# Why Aššur is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right
There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *ashur*. This is the file on how **Aššur** replaced it.

Aššur's mythology is inseparable from Assyrian royal ideology. The king is his vicar; the empire is his estate; the annual campaign is an act of worship. The stories are told not in narrative epics but in royal inscriptions, temple hymns, and the state theology of a nation at war. Assyrian scribes produced a version of the Babylonian Enuma Eliš in which Aššur, not Marduk, slays Tiamat and receives the fifty names of kingship.  The text transfers cosmic supremacy from Babylon's god to Assyria's god, making Aššur the creator and king of all gods.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Aššur
- **ASCII form:** ashur
- **Meaning:** "National god of Assyria (Akkadian Aššur)"
- **Domain of influence:** War, Kingship, Assyrian Patron
- **Pantheon:** Mesopotamian
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒀸𒋩
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 37 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

**Aššur** preserves its form without added diacritics: the restoration here is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form the tradition's own sources record. *ashur* and **Aššur** may look interchangeable to a search box; they are not interchangeable to a philologist.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Aššur** lives at [/sites/ashur/](/sites/ashur/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/ashur/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/ashur/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/ashur/patterns/).

The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can say — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it in Tier-1: mechanically verifiable, information-rich.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Aššur** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Defense, Military & Security** — The god who is the nation, whose sovereignty travels with the army — patron of archers and chariots, empire made deity.
- **Leadership, Governance & Public Administration** — The national god of an empire; Assyria governed in his name.
- **Ancestry & Heritage Services** — An entire people kept his name; Assyrian heritage communities still orbit the old god.

This is the part of the file that surprises people: a four-thousand-year-old name, mapping cleanly onto twenty-first-century trades. The patterns are not marketing — they are the same myths, read forward.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Mesopotamian tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Enūma Eliš](/texts/enuma-elish/) and [The Epic of Gilgamesh](/texts/gilgamesh/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
